demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is a poor fit unless the death involved clear interpersonal wrongdoing by a trusted person; nothing else in the profile supports that specific circumstance, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'Need to stay alert' at bedtime implies ongoing external danger, which is less coherent with bereavement-related trauma in the absence of any triggers or appraisals about current interpersonal/physical threat. The rest of the profile centers on loss, self-blame, fragmented reliving memory, and catastrophic interpretations of delay, making this item stand out as mismatched.

vignette:
Amina was twenty-one when her younger brother, Malik, drowned at a lake during a family outing. She had been tasked with watching him while their parents set up lunch, but she had glanced at a work email from her environmental science internship—just for a moment. By the time she looked up, Malik had waded too far and slipped under the surface. Paramedics revived him on the shore, but he died at the hospital that evening. Amina has never stopped believing that somebody else—a more responsible sister—would have stopped it. That conviction, along with her deepening sense that she is simply the sort of person who lets tragedy happen, now drives her daily life. Because she believed her inattention had cost Malik his life, Amina began refusing any work assignment that required her to supervise junior staff or volunteers near water — backing out of a river-sampling trip even though it meant disappointing her supervisor. She replays the afternoon over and over, blaming herself for every second of inattention, telling herself that what happened was profoundly unfair and that no one has been held accountable.

In the months after Malik’s death, each time she tried to recall the exact moment she looked up from her phone, the memory would vanish before it completed—she found herself pushing it away, unable to find words to describe the frozen terror she still felt. Yet the memory also felt entirely present, as if she were still standing on that lakeshore. The more she tried to avoid it, the more it intruded. Today, at twenty-three, Amina works as an environmental scientist, a job that often sends her to field sites near rivers and reservoirs. When a sample result arrives later than expected, her stomach drops—she is certain something catastrophic is happening again. Her heart races, her palms sweat, and she rarely has time to name the fear before her body reacts. These bodily surges often trigger a sudden, unbidden image of Malik’s face under water, and that flashback makes the danger feel immediate all over again, as though she is about to lose him a second time. She interprets every startle as proof that the world is still unfair, that she is indeed the kind of person bad things happen to.

At work, Amina has begun picking arguments with colleagues—snapping at a lab technician over a minor scheduling change, challenging a supervisor on a procedural detail. The conflict distracts her from the trauma for an hour or two, but afterwards she feels even more convinced that she is a difficult, unworthy person. Avoiding television shows or news stories about drowning takes constant effort, and the suppression often backfires: the memory surfaces with greater intensity, and she lies awake at night replaying what she could have done differently, her sleep growing more broken with each passing week. The rumination itself makes her feel vulnerable to further tragedy, so she jumps at small sounds in the lab. She has come to believe that her own hypervigilance is simply further evidence that she is fundamentally flawed. That belief made her feel perpetually unsafe — as though the flaw inside her was a magnet for disaster, and she could not walk into any room without sensing its approach. When the threat felt that close, replaying the afternoon in her head each night wasn't a choice — it was the only way she knew to keep any future disaster from sneaking up on her.

Amina recently sought therapy because her sleep deprivation and workplace conflicts led to a formal warning from her supervisor. She is exhausted, her relationships strained, and she fears that the guilt will never lift. What she hopes, more than anything, is to find a way out of the loop—to stop believing that she is the reason Malik died, and to quiet the body that keeps telling her another disaster is coming.
